strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: natural-language-controllable editing of real driving videos for synthesizing diverse and safety-critical traffic scenarios.

The system design is clear and well motivated: it decomposes driving videos into a scene graph, coordinates specialized agents/tools via an orchestrator, and adds diffusion-based refinement for photorealism and temporal coherence.

The framework supports a useful set of editing operations, including object removal, insertion, replacement, multi-object behavior editing, and ego-view trajectory changes, which is broader than several prior systems.

The empirical results consistently favor the proposed method over Cosmos and ChatSim across multiple reported metrics, including FID/FVD, instruction alignment, structure preservation, traffic violations, and user study preference.

The supplementary material provides useful ablations on the object grounding agent, behavior refinement loop, counterfactual behavior generation, unreasonable-instruction rejection, and video diffusion refinement.
Qualitative examples illustrate several desirable capabilities, such as adapting inserted objects to scene lighting and handling multi-object interactions in challenging nighttime conditions.
The paper documents prompts, scene IDs, implementation details, and failure cases, which improves transparency and helps the reader understand the pipeline.
The limitations section and failure-case discussion are a positive signal, especially the acknowledgment of pedestrian-editing limitations and video-diffusion-induced appearance changes.
weaknesses: If assessed as Algorithms/General, the algorithmic novelty is limited: most core modules rely on off-the-shelf components (3DGS reconstruction, LangTraj, Hunyuan3D, CogVideoX, GPT-4/4o, SAM, Grounding DINO) and the contribution is mainly system orchestration plus prompt/rule engineering. Framed as Applied/Systems, the integration is more compelling, but the paper should make that contribution type clearer.

The evaluation is restricted to 30 Waymo scenes, front-camera video, mostly vehicle editing, 8-second clips at 10 FPS, and only two empirical baselines despite a broader related-work landscape. There is no downstream evaluation showing that the generated data improves autonomous-driving training or validation.

Several important metrics rely on GPT-4o/VLM judgments, e.g., appearance alignment, collision rate, and off-road rate in the main table. These judgments may miss temporal violations, are not audited against ground-truth geometry, and make the claims less objective than geometric evaluation would.

The behavior refinement ablation reveals that harder multi-object instructions still yield only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates even after refinement. This is high for safety-critical simulation and weakens the traffic-realism claim.

The main-table traffic-violation numbers (0.58% collision, 1.73% off-road) appear inconsistent with the ablation results, likely because they are measured on easier instructions and/or via a weaker VLM-based protocol. This inconsistency should be explained and reconciled.

The video diffusion refinement can alter inserted object type or color (e.g., a green convertible becoming a black sedan), directly undermining instruction alignment and controllability. This is acknowledged as a failure case, but it affects a core claimed capability.

Reproducibility is only partial: the pipeline depends on proprietary GPT-4/4o agents and nondeterministic LLM/VLM decisions, and the video-diffusion finetuning data/details are not fully specified. Code release and compute/API requirements are unclear.

The method assumes access to original object trajectories and map information, so it is not purely video-based editing. Open-vocabulary querying is evaluated on only 50 queries from 5 scenes, and pedestrian/cyclist editing is explicitly not supported, limiting safety-critical coverage.

The paper overstates comparisons to prior state of the art in places: the 'nearly 2x higher instruction alignment' claim is based on custom VLM-based metrics and a limited baseline set, without confidence intervals or statistical significance testing.

The user study is relatively small (26 participants) and reports only preference percentages; recruitment, instructions, and uncertainty are not detailed, making the human evaluation less convincing than it could be.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: language-controllable editing of real-world driving videos for synthetic scenario generation.
The modular agentic design is coherent, combining explicit scene-graph-based editing with diffusion-based video refinement to balance controllability and photorealism.
Supports a useful range of operations: removal, insertion, replacement, multi-object behavior editing, and ego-view editing, which broadens utility for safety-critical scenario generation.
Quantitative results on 30 Waymo scenes show improvements over Cosmos and ChatSim in FID/FVD, instruction alignment, structure preservation, traffic realism, and user study.
The paper provides supplementary details including prompts, implementation settings, additional ablations, and failure cases, which improves transparency relative to many system papers.
Qualitative examples demonstrate challenging scenarios (nighttime, cut-in, feedback-loop refinement), suggesting practical potential if validation were stronger.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the framework is largely an orchestration of existing components (OmniRe/3DGS, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, CogVideoX/TrajectoryCrafter, GPT-4/4o); the proposed agents are prompt/heuristic wrappers rather than new algorithms or learned models.

Evaluation is insufficient for the broad SOTA claims: only 30 front-camera Waymo scenes and two baselines (Cosmos, ChatSim), with no quantitative comparison to other relevant language-controllable or scene-editing methods (e.g., DriveEditor, SceneCrafter, AutoVFX, ChatDyn, SimSplat).

Several metrics are unreliable or inadequately validated, especially using GPT-4o to judge appearance alignment, collisions, and off-road incidents from edited videos; no human agreement, ground-truth physical checks, or statistical significance tests are reported.

Behavior alignment evaluation uses the paper's own heuristic behavior-description logic, which is also used inside the reviewer/refinement loop; this risks circularity and may inflate improvements relative to baselines.

Input assumptions are restrictive: the method requires a scene map and original object trajectories, yet the framing emphasizes real-world driving videos; it also does not model pedestrians and fails on median barriers and uncommon inserted vehicles.

The video diffusion tool's training data and train/test split are not specified; it is unclear whether fine-tuning uses the same Waymo scenes or distribution, raising reproducibility and potential leakage concerns.

Ablations cover only behavior refinement, video refinement, counterfactual generation, and object grounding, but not the orchestrator, insertion agent, or reviewer design choices; sample sizes are small and improvements lack confidence intervals.

The reported failure cases (inserted vehicle changes type/color; driving on median barriers) directly contradict strong instruction-alignment/traffic-realism claims, and their frequency is not quantified in the main results.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on closed GPT-4/GPT-4o APIs, unspecified fine-tuning data, and no released code/model details; prompt-based components are likely brittle across VLM/LLM versions.

The paper overstates agent novelty: multi-agent orchestration, LLM-based reviewing, and iterative refinement are well-established ideas, and the manuscript does not sufficiently isolate a novel technical insight beyond system integration.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel, well-motivated framework for natural-language-controllable driving scene editing by combining explicit 3D scene graph decomposition with an LLM/VLM agentic orchestration. It supports removal, insertion, replacement, ego-view edits, and multi-object behavior editing, going beyond many prior systems.

The proposed Object Grounding Agent, Behavior Editing Agent, and Behavior Reviewer Agent form a coherent pipeline, and the reviewer feedback loop is a sensible mechanism for improving trajectory-instruction alignment and traffic compliance.

The experimental suite is comparatively broad: quantitative comparisons on photorealism, instruction alignment, structure preservation, and traffic realism; a user study; multiple ablations; and qualitative examples on challenging day/night scenes.

The supplementary material provides substantial implementation detail, including prompts, behavior description heuristics, counterfactual mapping/compatibility rules, and test scene IDs, which aids reproducibility and clarifies system design.
The paper demonstrates clear practical potential for generating diverse, safety-critical driving scenarios from real-world logs, an important problem for autonomous driving simulation and validation.
Ablations show that both the behavior refinement loop and video diffusion refinement contribute measurably to performance, supporting the paper's design choices.
The work is generally well structured, and the related-work comparison table helps position the contributions against prior editing capacities.
weaknesses: The traffic-realism evidence is inconsistent. Table 1 reports very low VLM-measured collision/off-road rates for Ours (0.58%/1.73%), but the trajectory-level ablation in Table 2 reports 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road after the refinement loop, with overall success only 51.43%. This discrepancy calls into question the reliability of the final-video VLM evaluation and weakens the claim of strong traffic realism.

Evaluation is limited to 30 front-camera Waymo scenes, 8 seconds at 10 FPS, and primarily vehicles; no pedestrian editing or broader dataset/sensor validation is shown, so generalization is uncertain.

Key instruction-alignment and traffic-realism metrics rely on GPT-4o/VLM judgments, which can be noisy, prompt-sensitive, and costly. There is no validation against human labels or ground-truth trajectories for those metrics, and the user study (26 participants, best-choice only) is not a substitute for rigorous metric validation.

The baseline comparison includes only Cosmos and ChatSim, despite several related editing methods (DriveEditor, SceneCrafter, AutoVFX, ChatDyn, SimSplat) being discussed. Full-pipeline comparisons are missing, so the claimed state-of-the-art advantage is not fully established.

As Algorithms/General work, the algorithmic novelty is partly system integration: many core capabilities come from existing pretrained modules (3DGS/OmniRe, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, CogVideoX, GPT-4/4o, TrajectoryCrafter). The new agent components are largely prompt- and heuristic-based, which may limit technical depth and robustness.

Reproducibility is hampered by reliance on proprietary LLM APIs and large external models. Although the authors provide prompts, they do not provide code/data release, and fine-tuning plus evaluation details for the video diffusion tool and VLM-based metrics are abbreviated.

The behavior editing logic uses hand-crafted counterfactual mappings and compatibility constraints (Tables 10/11), which may not generalize to complex intersections, unusual road topologies, or dense multi-agent interactions. Some failure cases, such as driving on a median barrier, are acknowledged.

The video refinement module can alter inserted-object identity/appearance (green convertible becomes black sedan), so object-level fidelity is not guaranteed, and the paper does not quantify how often this occurs beyond one failure example.

Some qualitative examples use unaligned timestamps and selective frames, and the photorealism gain over Cosmos in FID (32.85 vs 33.42) is modest; claims of significant photorealism superiority should be interpreted carefully.

strengths: Introduces a comprehensive feedback-driven agentic framework that unifies explicit 3D scene-graph representation with natural-language control for driving video editing, supporting removal, insertion, replacement, multi-object behavior editing, and ego-view editing.

Combines multi-modal agents (orchestrator, object grounding, behavior editing/reviewing, video reviewing) with specialized tools, and provides detailed prompts and implementation descriptions in the supplementary material, improving interpretability.

Reports strong empirical gains over Cosmos and ChatSim across photorealism, instruction alignment, structure preservation, and traffic realism, including nearly 2x higher appearance/behavior alignment and large user-study preference.

Includes extensive ablations on object grounding, counterfactual behavior generation, behavior refinement, video refinement, and unreasonable-instruction rejection, plus a downstream BEVFormer detection study and failure-case/hallucination analyses.
Maintains comparable runtime to prior SoTA methods while handling a wide set of editing capabilities, making it a practically relevant systems-level contribution.
weaknesses: Originality is largely integrative: the method chains existing off-the-shelf components (3DGS, GPT-4/4o, SAM, Grounding SAM, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, CogVideoX/TrajectoryCrafter) with rule-based behavior tables and prompt-driven agents, so the core technical novelty beyond orchestration and feedback loops is limited.
Heavy reliance on proprietary LLM/VLM APIs and multiple large models raises reproducibility, cost, and latency concerns; API/token usage is not reported, and code/model release is not promised.

Evaluation is relatively limited: only 30 Waymo scenes are used, object grounding is evaluated on 50 queries with a lenient IoU>0.2 success threshold, and the human study has only 26 participants without statistical testing.

Behavior refinement still leaves substantial failures on challenging multi-object instructions (51.43% overall success, 22.86% collision rate), and the paper does not deeply analyze when/why the VLM-based reviewers fail.

Baseline comparison is narrow: only Cosmos, ChatSim, and a naive image-editing+image-to-video baseline are empirically compared, while several related methods in Table 12 are not tested; SoTA claims therefore rest on a small evaluation set.

Some experimental details are underspecified, including FID/FVD computation protocol, video diffusion fine-tuning data, and appearance-alignment VLM judging; there are also minor citation/table inconsistencies (e.g., Cosmos incorrectly referenced as [9] in Table 1).

strengths: Addresses an important problem: natural-language-controllable editing of real driving videos for synthetic data generation, with support for removal, insertion, replacement, and multi-object behavior editing.
Builds a comprehensive scene-graph-based agentic pipeline that integrates 3D reconstruction, object grounding, trajectory simulation, rendering, and diffusion refinement into a unified workflow.

The feedback loops are intuitively motivated and ablated: behavior reviewer improves overall trajectory success from 34.29% to 51.43%, while video reviewer recovers appearance alignment from 65.47% to 85.28% after diffusion harmonization.

Reports large gains in instruction alignment over baselines (Appearance 82.19% vs. 46.25%/42.33%; Behavior 71.67% vs. 32.86%/26.64%) and better user-study preference, with comparable per-edit latency.

Qualitative examples show diverse and challenging edits, including nighttime insertion, ego-view changes, and multi-object lane changes, demonstrating the system's capabilities beyond single-object editing.
Includes a downstream 3D detection experiment suggesting edited data can augment real data, and supplementary material provides detailed prompts and implementation notes.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the framework largely combines off-the-shelf components such as GPT-4/4o, OmniRe/3DGS, LangTraj, Hunyuan3D, CogVideoX, and TrajectoryCrafter, while the agents are mainly prompt engineering plus heuristic feedback rather than new technical contributions.

Evaluation is limited in scale and scope: only 30 Waymo scenes, front-camera videos, and mostly vehicle editing. Baselines are restricted to Cosmos, ChatSim, and one naive image-edit plus image-to-video pipeline, despite many related editing methods being discussed but not quantitatively compared.

Several key metrics rely on GPT-4o judgments of instruction alignment, collisions, and off-road behavior without validation of the VLM evaluator against human or trajectory-level ground truth, raising serious reliability and bias concerns.

Absolute performance remains weak in important aspects: behavior refinement attains only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates in the ablation; a failure case drives over a median barrier, indicating unresolved traffic-realism issues.

Hallucination analysis shows that the video diffusion refinement degrades 3D consistency and lane structure preservation (3D consistency 74.07 to 72.64; NTL-IoU 52.11 to 50.96), while the coarse video has higher appearance alignment than the refined video without review, exposing a realism-preservation trade-off.

Reproducibility is questionable: the method depends on proprietary APIs, expensive fine-tuning (reported 4xH100 for 96 hours), and no code/data/model release is indicated. Training data for the video diffusion tool and potential overlap with test scenes are not sufficiently specified.

The grounding evaluation uses only 50 queries and considers IoU > 0.2 as success, which is low; the user study has only 26 participants with limited protocol detail, and no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported.

Presentation contains careless citation/reference errors, e.g., Table 1 cites Cosmos as [9] while the text uses [3]; Table 12 cites OminiRe as [18] when reference [18] is Grad-PU; and references [64,65] appear unrelated to the driving-editing context.

Practical efficiency is underwhelming: 17.1 minutes per edit plus around 2 hours of one-time reconstruction per scene, making large-scale data generation costly. The downstream detection gains are small and lack significance analysis.
The method assumes access to original object trajectories and map information, which may not be available in many real-world driving videos, limiting the claimed applicability to arbitrary footage.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: natural-language-controllable editing of real driving videos for synthetic data generation, combining explicit scene-graph representations with diffusion-based rendering refinement.

Presents a comprehensive agentic system with an orchestrator, object grounding agent, behavior editing agent, behavior reviewer, and video reviewer; supports removal, insertion, replacement, and multi-object behavior editing.

Reports strong empirical improvements across multiple axes: nearly 2x higher instruction alignment, better FID/FVD, structure preservation, and traffic realism, supported by a user study and multiple ablations.
The feedback-driven iterative refinement of behavior and video is well motivated and validated through ablation studies; hallucination analysis and downstream detection experiments add credibility.
The paper is generally clear and detailed, with extensive implementation details, prompts, and a failure-case discussion.
The system's performance is shown to stem from the core architecture, not only the video diffusion refinement, via the Ours (Coarse) vs. ChatSim experiment.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is mostly system integration of existing components (GPT-4/4o, 3DGS, LangTraj, CogVideoX, Hunyuan3D, SAM/Grounded-SAM); the core algorithmic contribution beyond orchestration and feedback loops is limited.
Evaluation is somewhat narrow: 30 Waymo scenes, vehicle-centric editing, limited pedestrian/cyclist coverage, and no cross-dataset generalization or statistical significance/variance reporting.

Several key evaluation metrics rely on VLM/LLM judgments (appearance alignment, collision/off-road detection), which may be biased or circular given that GPT-4o is also used inside the pipeline; more independent verification would strengthen the claims.
Absolute behavior-editing success remains modest after refinement (51.43% overall success, 22.86% collision, 14.29% off-road), which tempers the traffic-realism claim despite outperforming baselines.
Reproducibility is a concern: heavy reliance on proprietary APIs, substantial compute (2-hour preprocessing, 17-minute edit, 4xH100 fine-tuning), and no explicit code release or artifact statement.

The object grounding ablation uses only 50 queries with a lenient IoU>0.2 success criterion, and the downstream detection gains are small and lack comparison to other synthetic-data augmentation strategies.
The method assumes provided object trajectories and maps, and robustness to reconstruction failures, occlusions, large viewpoint changes, and non-vehicle dynamic agents is not fully explored.
